title: Manetti Shrem Museum: Together Again, 1960–2026, Perspectives from UC Davis’ Fine Arts Collection
location: Jan Shrem and Maria Manetti Shrem Museum of Art at UC Davis, 254 Old Davis Road, Davis, CA, 95616, United States
description:
Together Again inaugurates the Manetti Shrem Museum’s ongoing collection galleries. This exhibition highlighting the collection will be on long-term view, accompanied by temporary exhibitions each fall and winter. 
The ongoing collection galleries trace a history of art forged from UC Davis and throughout Northern California. By focusing on relationships of many kinds, this presentation proposes that in order to understand an artwork in all its fullness, chance encounters and long-standing friendships often matter as much as formal affiliations. UC Davis legends such as Wayne Thiebaud, Deborah Butterfield and Bruce Nauman are exhibited alongside important regional voices that were once overlooked, and the exhibition extends to the artists shaping Northern California today, including Sadie Barnette, Woody De Othello and Ruby Neri. Together Again builds bridges between who we were and who we are becoming at UC Davis, and affirms the Manetti Shrem Museum as home to the complex story of Northern California art — rich in legacy and always in the process of becoming. 
The collection will be open Wednesdays to Sundays, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. The location is the Jan Shrem and Maria Manetti Shrem Museum of Art at UC Davis. Admission is free.

title: Above Bone
location: Axis Gallery, 625 S St, Sacramento, 95811, United States
description:
ADERO WILLARD
ABOVE BONE
November 6–29, 2026 
Reception and Artist Talk on Saturday, November 7, 5–8 PM
Artist in the gallery on Sundays, November 8 and 29, 12–5 PM 
Axis Gallery presents Above Bone, an exhibition of ceramic sculpture by Sacramento artist Adero Willard, on view November 6 through 29, 2026. The exhibition brings together new work and pieces never before shown in Sacramento or on the West Coast. Join the artist for the reception and artist talk on Saturday, November 7, 5–8 PM. 
ABOUT THE EXHIBITION
Above Bone refers to what is beneath, the layers, and what emerges. Clay sculptural vessels of heads and body forms explore death, regeneration, new growth, and what is hidden. Adero wrestles clay into expressive forms and creates surfaces dense in color and pattern: thick clay and delicately etched vines and flowers. The forms are camouflaged, as if growing from or being returned to the ground. Layered colorful patterns, resists, and luster build up over multiple firings. Pattern is masked, peeled back, and built up again, so each surface both hides and reveals. The work is rooted in the earth and in a mixed ancestry: ancestors from this land and from lands never touched, removed from the land by history and time. It reflects a search for grounding, authenticity, and belonging. These pieces hold quiet conversations with personal history, our current history, and ancestors.
The exhibition moves through memory, death, decay, and renewal. Patterns are hidden, revealed, and peeled; color surfaces from shadow. Drawing on textiles, flowers, plants, and insects, the work asks what grows from decay. New work appears alongside pieces making their Sacramento debut. 
ABOUT THE ARTIST 
Adero Willard (they/them/she/her) is a ceramic artist, educator, and curator whose work explores surface, identity, and cultural memory through clay. Born in New York City, Willard earned a BFA from the New York State College of Ceramics at Alfred University and an MFA from the Nova Scotia College of Art and Design in Halifax, Canada. They have exhibited and lectured nationally and internationally and have been featured in numerous publications and books on contemporary ceramics. 
Currently Assistant Professor of Ceramics at California State University, Sacramento, Willard is also a co-founder of Pots on Wheels!, a nonprofit dedicated to expanding access to clay through community-based programs across the U.S. Willard’s artistic, teaching, 
and curatorial practices are grounded in a commitment to equity and to advocating for more inclusive institutional and cultural frameworks that reflect the richness and diversity of the field.

title: Capturing Memories of Grief/Capturando Memorias del Duelo
location: Axis Gallery, 625 S St, Sacramento, 95811, United States
description:
SUMMER VENTIS AND LINA RINCÓN
CAPTURING MEMORIES OF GRIEF/CAPTURANDO MEMORIAS DEL DUELO
November 6–29, 2026 
Reception on Saturday, November 7, 5–8 PM 
The project, “Capturing Memories of Grief,” is a collaboration between artist Summer Ventis, sociologist and poet Lina Rincón, and you. Together, we explore the intersection of grief, memory, and image. 
We began this project with a conversation about our shared experience of losing a parent. When we recalled these experiences, we learned that we both had memories that centered around images, photographs, and the process of photography as a way to make sense of and process the meanings of our loss. 
In Fall of 2025, we began a series of grief-themed tours of works in the Crocker Art Museum’s collection. At the end of the tours, participants gathered to share and document our memories of grief and loss and how they connect with different types of images. We invited participants to consider grief and loss broadly; while we first connected around the death of family members, death is not the only kind of loss or the only thing we grieve. We encouraged participants to reflect on different experiences of grief and loss, the images they associated with them, and their feelings around these images. 
This exhibition is a collection of the artifacts of these exchanges, an opportunity to collect our experiences and reflect on them together. 
/ 
El proyecto “Capturando memorias del duelo,” es un proyecto colaborativo entre la artista Summer Ventis, la socióloga y poeta Lina Rincón y usted. Juntes, exploramos la intersección del duelo, la memoria y la imágen.
Este proyecto comenzó con una conversación sobre nuestra experiencia compartida de perder a uno de nuestros parientes. Cuando recordamos estas experiencias, nos dimos cuenta que para darle sentido a los significados del duelo y procesarlos, relatamos memorias que centraban imágenes, fotografías, y el proceso de la fotografía. 
En el otoño del 2025, empezamos una serie de recorridos de las obras de arte del Museo Crocker centrando el tema del duelo. Al final del recorrido, los participantes compartieron y documentaron sus experiencias con memorias del duelo y sus conexiones con diferentes tipos de imágenes. En el recorrido, invitamos a los participantes a considerar las experiencias del duelo y la pérdida de manera amplia; aunque es común pensar en la muerte de nuestros familiares primero, la muerte no es la única manera de pensar en las experiencias de duelo y pérdida. De este modo, motivamos a los participantes a reflexionar sobre sus diferentes experiencias con el duelo y la pérdida, las imagenes que elles asociaron con esta experiencias, y los sentimientos alrededor de estas imagenes. 
Esta exhibición es una colección de los artefactos de estos intercambios, una oportunidad para recolectar nuestras experiencias, y también para reflexionar sobre ellas. 
ABOUT THE ARTIST 
Summer Ventis 
Summer Ventis’s work uses the printed surface to address internal and external landscapes and their intersections; the imprints we leave on each other and our surroundings and the imprints that our surroundings leave on us. She received a BA in Art from Grinnell College and an MFA in Printmaking from the University of Colorado Boulder. Her work has appeared in national and international exhibitions, and is held by collections including those of the Denver Art Museum and Proyecto ’ace in Buenos Aires, Argentina. She is a member of the Colorado-based collectives Hyperlink and ARTNAUTS and of Sacramento-based Axis Gallery and is Associate Professor of Printmaking at California State University Sacramento. 
Lina Rincón
An immigrant herself, Lina Rincón studies the experiences of migrant workers in the U.S. As part of her research, Lina has revealed the detrimental effect different visa programs and associated policies have on families. This includes family temporary or permanent family separation. Lina also brings her artistry as a published poet who has captured experiences of loss and change in immigrant families in her poetry. She received a BA and a Masters Degree in Anthropology from Universidad de los Andes in Bogotá, Colombia and a PhD in Sociology from the State University of New York at Albany. She is Associate Professor of Sociology at California State University Sacramento.

La obra de Summer Ventis usa la superficie impresa para revelar paisajes internos y externos y sus intersecciones; las impresiones que dejamos en cada une de nosotres y nuestros alrededores y las impresiones que nuestros alrededores dejan en nosotres. Summer recibió su BA en artes de Grinnell College y un MFA en grabado de la Universidad de Colorado en Boulder. Su arte ha aparecido en exhibiciones nacionales e internacionales y ha sido adquirido por varias colecciones, incluyendo las del Museo de Arte de Denver y el Proyecto ’ace en Buenos Aires, Argentina. Summer hace parte de los colectivos Hyperlink y ARTNAUTS, basados en Colorado, y de la Galería Axis, basada en Sacramento. Summer es profesora asociada de grabado en la Universidad Estatal de California en Sacramento.

Como inmigrante que es, Lina Rincón estudia las experiencias de trabajadores migrantes en los Estados Unidos. Como parte de su investigación, Lina ha revelado los efectos perjudiciales que diferentes programas de visas de inmigración y sus políticas asociadas tienen en las familias inmigrantes. Estos efectos incluyen la separación temporal o permanente de miembros de estas familias. Lina es también una poeta que ha capturado experiencias de dolor y cambio en las experiencias de familias inmigrantes en su poesía. Lina recibió su BA y maestría en antropología de la Universidad de los Andes en Bogotá, Colombia y su PhD en sociología de la Universidad Estatal de Nueva York en Albany. Our selection, On Tyranny: Twenty Lessons from the Twentieth Century by Timothy Snyder is a call to arms and a guide to resistance, with invaluable ideas for how we can preserve our freedoms in the uncertain years to come. The Founding Fathers tried to protect us from the threat they knew, the tyranny that overcame ancient democracy. Today, our political order faces new threats, not unlike the totalitarianism of the twentieth century. We are no wiser than the Europeans who saw democracy yield to fascism, Nazism, or communism. Our one advantage is that we might learn from their experience. Author Timothy Snyder holds the inaugural Temerty Chair in Modern European History at the Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy at the University of Toronto. title: Freedom of Expression at UC Davis: Know Your Rights
description:
Ever wondered where the line is between free speech, campus policy, and taking a stand? Whether you're planning a demonstration, organizing an event with your RSO, or just navigating lively debates around campus, knowing your rightsis key.

Join CSI's Assistant Director for Student Expression, Jose Napoles, for an interactive breakdown of what Freedom of Expression actually looks like on campus. We’ll clear up the confusion around campus forums, break down time, place, and manner policies, and give you the tools to make informed decisions and keep your communities safe.

In this session, you’ll learn how to:

Know Your Forums: Understand the difference between public, limited, and nonpublic spaces on campus and how your rights shift in each.

Decode Campus Policies: Get the real scoop on policy boundaries like amplified sound, tabling, and event security so your events run smoothly.

Protect & Advocate: Discover how the Student Affairs Response Team supports student expression, helps de-escalate tension, and connects you with key campus resources.

Navigate Real Scenarios: Work through practical examples of campus dissent and learn proactive strategies for community safety and self-care.

Who should attend? Student organization leaders, campus advocates, and any Aggie who wants to speak up, stay informed, and make an impact effectively.

Bring your questions and come learn more about Freedom of Expression at UC Davis.

*SPACE IS LIMITED!*

title: Manetti Shrem Museum: Together Again, 1960–2026, Perspectives from UC Davis’ Fine Arts Collection
location: Jan Shrem and Maria Manetti Shrem Museum of Art at UC Davis, 254 Old Davis Road, Davis, CA, 95616, United States
description:
Together Again inaugurates the Manetti Shrem Museum’s ongoing collection galleries. This exhibition highlighting the collection will be on long-term view, accompanied by temporary exhibitions each fall and winter. 
The ongoing collection galleries trace a history of art forged from UC Davis and throughout Northern California. By focusing on relationships of many kinds, this presentation proposes that in order to understand an artwork in all its fullness, chance encounters and long-standing friendships often matter as much as formal affiliations. UC Davis legends such as Wayne Thiebaud, Deborah Butterfield and Bruce Nauman are exhibited alongside important regional voices that were once overlooked, and the exhibition extends to the artists shaping Northern California today, including Sadie Barnette, Woody De Othello and Ruby Neri. Together Again builds bridges between who we were and who we are becoming at UC Davis, and affirms the Manetti Shrem Museum as home to the complex story of Northern California art — rich in legacy and always in the process of becoming. 
The collection will be open Wednesdays to Sundays, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. The location is the Jan Shrem and Maria Manetti Shrem Museum of Art at UC Davis. Admission is free.

title: Manetti Shrem Museum: Together Again, 1960–2026, Perspectives from UC Davis’ Fine Arts Collection
location: Jan Shrem and Maria Manetti Shrem Museum of Art at UC Davis, 254 Old Davis Road, Davis, CA, 95616, United States
description:
Together Again inaugurates the Manetti Shrem Museum’s ongoing collection galleries. This exhibition highlighting the collection will be on long-term view, accompanied by temporary exhibitions each fall and winter. 
The ongoing collection galleries trace a history of art forged from UC Davis and throughout Northern California. By focusing on relationships of many kinds, this presentation proposes that in order to understand an artwork in all its fullness, chance encounters and long-standing friendships often matter as much as formal affiliations. UC Davis legends such as Wayne Thiebaud, Deborah Butterfield and Bruce Nauman are exhibited alongside important regional voices that were once overlooked, and the exhibition extends to the artists shaping Northern California today, including Sadie Barnette, Woody De Othello and Ruby Neri. Together Again builds bridges between who we were and who we are becoming at UC Davis, and affirms the Manetti Shrem Museum as home to the complex story of Northern California art — rich in legacy and always in the process of becoming. 
The collection will be open Wednesdays to Sundays, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. The location is the Jan Shrem and Maria Manetti Shrem Museum of Art at UC Davis. Admission is free.

Register in advance for the Zoom link. This helps us connect you to the right expert for your question.

In addition to DataLab, the collaborative data science office hours are supported by:

Biostatistics (Clinical and Translational Science Center, CTSC)Computational Research Data Service (College of Letters & Science)High Performance Computing (HPC) CoreResearcher Services (UC Davis Library)Stat Lab (Department of Statistics)Common office hours help topics include:

Open Source Programming (R, Python, Julia, etc.)Reproducible research computing and data scienceResponsible and ethical data scienceData gathering, organization, databases, and experimental designData analysis, statistics, and explorationData visualizationMachine learning and neural networksText mining and natural language processingGeospatial sciencesRemote and high performance computingComputational pedagogy… and more!Please note that drop-in office hours are not offered during University holidays, academic breaks and finals week. Summer schedule varies based on availability.

title: Un-Coding AI in the Classroom: 2-Day Workshop for Faculty and Instructors
location: DataLab Classroom, Shields Library, 360
description:
Generative AI is reshaping the landscape of higher education, raising important questions for teaching, learning, and academic integrity. Designed for faculty and instructors across all disciplines and requiring no prior technical background, this two-day workshop unpacks genAI and offers practical strategies for the university classroom. Whether you are curious about how these models work, eager to integrate AI into your teaching, or cautious about its impact on student learning, this series offers a supportive, nuanced space to explore. Participants will gain a clear foundational understanding of large language models (LLMs), evaluate the opportunities and limitations of genAI, and engage in hands-on practice configuring customized and privacy-protected AI learning environments for their courses.

 

The workshop runs Thursday-Friday December 10-11 from 9 AM - 4 PM daily with a break for lunch. Full participation in both days is recommended as topics build across sessions.

 

Day 1: Un-coding AI

Day 1 strips away the technical jargon to examine what genAI actually is — and what it isn't. Taking a no-code approach, we begin by exploring how LLMs process and generate language using intuitive, non-mathematical concepts. We examine how these models are developed and generate responses, explore the root causes of hallucinations, trace the influence of algorithmic bias, and discuss the impacts of genAI on the environment, society and self. 

 

Moving into practical engagement, we will discuss pedagogical and prompting strategies that keep human judgment and critical thinking firmly at the center of the learning process while safeguarding privacy. At the end of the day we will review institutional technology stack options (including the RockyAI implementation in Canvas, Google Gemini, and open-source models) to help you weigh the pros, cons, and privacy considerations as you build a practical roadmap for considering genAI integration into your courses.

 

Day 2: AI in the Classroom

Building on Day 1's foundational concepts, Day 2 transitions into an interactive, hands-on workshop focused on implementing privacy-protected AI tools directly into your curriculum. Participants will work step-by-step to configure course-ready environments on their own devices. We will explore an implementation of RockyAI embedded within Canvas for 24/7 student support grounded in instructor-approved course materials, set up local open-source models via Ollama to ensure complete data privacy and minimal environmental resource impact, and finally how to leverage the campus-licensed Google Gemini suite. By the end of this session, you will have functional AI tools set up for your courses along with the knowledge and confidence to guide your students in using them effectively to enhance their learning.

 

By participating in both days of this workshop, faculty and instructors will be able to:

Demystify Core Concepts: Explain the basic principles, capabilities, and limitations of large language models without relying on technical or mathematical jargon.

Validate & Evaluate Outputs: Apply systematic validation strategies to detect and explore hallucinations, bias, and factual inaccuracies in AI-generated content.

Articulate Impacts: Describe the environmental, social, cognitive and psychological impacts of genAI use and common teaching and learning pitfalls.

Navigate Campus Tech Stacks: Evaluate the privacy protections, costs, and practical trade-offs of various AI environments (including Canvas integrations, enterprise suites, and local models).

title: Un-Coding AI in the Classroom: 2-Day Workshop for Faculty and Instructors
location: DataLab Classroom, Shields Library, 360
description:
Generative AI is reshaping the landscape of higher education, raising important questions for teaching, learning, and academic integrity. Designed for faculty and instructors across all disciplines and requiring no prior technical background, this two-day workshop unpacks genAI and offers practical strategies for the university classroom. Whether you are curious about how these models work, eager to integrate AI into your teaching, or cautious about its impact on student learning, this series offers a supportive, nuanced space to explore. Participants will gain a clear foundational understanding of large language models (LLMs), evaluate the opportunities and limitations of genAI, and engage in hands-on practice configuring customized and privacy-protected AI learning environments for their courses.

 

The workshop runs Thursday-Friday December 10-11 from 9 AM - 4 PM daily with a break for lunch. Full participation in both days is recommended as topics build across sessions.

 

Day 1: Un-coding AI

Day 1 strips away the technical jargon to examine what genAI actually is — and what it isn't. Taking a no-code approach, we begin by exploring how LLMs process and generate language using intuitive, non-mathematical concepts. We examine how these models are developed and generate responses, explore the root causes of hallucinations, trace the influence of algorithmic bias, and discuss the impacts of genAI on the environment, society and self. 

 

Moving into practical engagement, we will discuss pedagogical and prompting strategies that keep human judgment and critical thinking firmly at the center of the learning process while safeguarding privacy. At the end of the day we will review institutional technology stack options (including the RockyAI implementation in Canvas, Google Gemini, and open-source models) to help you weigh the pros, cons, and privacy considerations as you build a practical roadmap for considering genAI integration into your courses.

 

Day 2: AI in the Classroom

Building on Day 1's foundational concepts, Day 2 transitions into an interactive, hands-on workshop focused on implementing privacy-protected AI tools directly into your curriculum. Participants will work step-by-step to configure course-ready environments on their own devices. We will explore an implementation of RockyAI embedded within Canvas for 24/7 student support grounded in instructor-approved course materials, set up local open-source models via Ollama to ensure complete data privacy and minimal environmental resource impact, and finally how to leverage the campus-licensed Google Gemini suite. By the end of this session, you will have functional AI tools set up for your courses along with the knowledge and confidence to guide your students in using them effectively to enhance their learning.

 

By participating in both days of this workshop, faculty and instructors will be able to:

Demystify Core Concepts: Explain the basic principles, capabilities, and limitations of large language models without relying on technical or mathematical jargon.

Validate & Evaluate Outputs: Apply systematic validation strategies to detect and explore hallucinations, bias, and factual inaccuracies in AI-generated content.

Articulate Impacts: Describe the environmental, social, cognitive and psychological impacts of genAI use and common teaching and learning pitfalls.

Navigate Campus Tech Stacks: Evaluate the privacy protections, costs, and practical trade-offs of various AI environments (including Canvas integrations, enterprise suites, and local models).

Deploy Privacy-Protected Tools: Configure and manage course-specific, privacy-focused AI assistants (such as Rocky AI, Google Gemini, and Ollama) to support student learning.

Design Pedagogy: Develop practical course-based roadmaps and effective prompting strategy examples to promote your student’s cognition, critical thinking, and academic integrity while protecting personal and institutional data.

Depending on the nature of your question and our availability, it may be possible to schedule a longer follow-up consultation after your office hours visit.

Common office hours help topics include:

Open Source Programming (R, Python, Julia, etc.)Reproducible research computing and data scienceResponsible and ethical data scienceData gathering, organization, databases, and experimental designData analysis, statistics, and explorationData visualizationMachine learning and neural networksText mining and natural language processingGeospatial sciencesRemote and high performance computingComputational pedagogy… and more!Please note that drop-in office hours are not offered during University holidays, academic breaks and finals week. Summer schedule varies. DataLab may only be accessed during Shields Library's business hours. Click here for detailed directions to DataLab.

Note: We are unable to provide support for assigned coursework (homework assignments, class projects, etc.) during office hours. If you need such help please contact your instructor or TA for assistance. If you need help with technical problems such system administration and hardware issues, check out the the UC Davis ServiceHub and/or contact your departmental IT.
